hypotheses.title: Direct swap price bounds never enforced when only BEFORE_SWAP hook flag is set
hypotheses.summary: When a token has TOKEN_SETTINGS_BEFORE_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG set but NOT TOKEN_SETTINGS_AFTER_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG, the price bounds check in AMMStandardHook._validatePricingBounds is never enforced for direct swaps. The beforeSwap path writes the slot then immediately returns (line 840) without any bounds check. The afterSwap path is never reached because the after-swap hook is not enabled. A trader can therefore execute a direct swap at any price — including arbitrarily worse prices — bypassing the token-configured sqrtPriceX96 bounds entirely.
hypotheses.victim: Token holders / LPs protected by AMMStandardHook price bounds
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Trader executes swap at price far outside configured bounds, extracting value from the pool or exploiting stale liquidity
hypotheses.mechanism: _validatePricingBounds line 840 `return` exits without bounds check when isBeforeSwap=true. The poolId==bytes32(0) branch is taken for direct swaps. Only when afterSwap is also enabled does the check ever run (lines 843-869). Flag check at beforeSwap entry (AMMModule._executeBeforeSwapHooks) only gates whether the hook is called at all — it does not gate bounds enforcement.

AMMStandardHook.sol: 840:     return;  // NO BOUNDS CHECK — exits immediately
854-869: // bounds check only executed in afterSwap path

attack_preconditions: Token must have TOKEN_SETTINGS_BEFORE_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG set (enabling before-swap hook)
Token must NOT have TOKEN_SETTINGS_AFTER_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG set (disabling after-swap hook)
Token must use AMMStandardHook with price bounds configured (non-zero sqrtPriceX96 min/max)
A direct swap pool must exist for the token
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker identifies token with AMMStandardHook configured with BEFORE_SWAP but not AFTER_SWAP hooks. 2. Token has tight price bounds set to protect LP from sandwich attacks. 3. Attacker calls directSwap with a large input, moving price far outside configured bounds. 4. No revert occurs — bounds check runs in afterSwap which is never triggered. 5. Attacker profits from arbitrage at an extreme price the hook was meant to prevent.
hypotheses.notes: This is a configuration-dependent bypass. The vulnerability exists for any token operator who inadvertently enables before-swap but not after-swap hooks while setting price bounds. The token setting manager role controls hook flags, so the attack surface depends on how tokens are configured in practice.

hypotheses.title: Permanent DoS for direct swaps when only AFTER_SWAP hook flag is set (zero-slot misread)
hypotheses.summary: When a token has TOKEN_SETTINGS_AFTER_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG set but NOT TOKEN_SETTINGS_BEFORE_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG, the DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT is never written in beforeSwap (hook not called). In afterSwap, _validatePricingBounds reads the uninitialized slot (value = 0). SqrtPriceCalculator.computeRatioX96 called with amount0=0 or amount1=0 returns MAX_SQRT_RATIO or MIN_SQRT_RATIO respectively. This triggers bounds check failure for any valid price bounds, permanently bricking all direct swaps for that token.
hypotheses.victim: Token users / protocol — all direct swaps for the affected token become permanently impossible
hypotheses.attacker_profit: DoS attack: attacker can configure a token (if they have LBAMM_TOKEN_SETTING_MANAGER_ROLE) to brick direct swaps, or operator misconfiguration creates permanent DoS
hypotheses.mechanism: In afterSwap: params.amount holds amountOut, _getTstorish(DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT) returns 0 (never written). computeRatioX96(0, amountOut) returns MIN_SQRT_RATIO or computeRatioX96(amountOut, 0) returns MAX_SQRT_RATIO. Both extreme values fail any reasonable sqrtPriceMin/sqrtPriceMax bounds check.
attack_preconditions: Token has TOKEN_SETTINGS_AFTER_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG set but NOT TOKEN_SETTINGS_BEFORE_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG
Price bounds are configured (sqrtPriceMin > MIN_SQRT_RATIO or sqrtPriceMax < MAX_SQRT_RATIO)
Direct swap attempted for this token
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Token operator (malicious or mistaken) sets AFTER_SWAP hook flag only on AMMStandardHook. 2. Any non-trivial price bounds are configured. 3. Every direct swap for this token now reads a zero slot in afterSwap, produces extreme ratio, fails bounds check, and reverts. 4. Direct swap functionality is permanently DoS'd for that token. If operator is malicious (rug), this freezes user ability to exit position.
hypotheses.notes: Related to H-transient-storage-01 — they form a symmetric pair of the flag asymmetry problem. H-01 is a bypass, H-02 is a DoS. The root cause is that the write and read are guarded by separate flags with no enforcement that both must be set together.

hypotheses.title: SSTORE fallback: DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT persists cross-transaction enabling price bounds manipulation
hypotheses.summary: In chains or environments where EIP-1153 (tstore/tload) is not supported and Tstorish falls back to sstore/sload, the DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) is never cleared after afterSwap reads it. The value persists to subsequent transactions. An attacker who can predict or influence the slot value from a prior transaction can manipulate the apparent amountIn that afterSwap sees, causing incorrect bounds computation.
hypotheses.victim: Token holders protected by AMMStandardHook price bounds in SSTORE fallback environments
hypotheses.attacker_profit: By carefully setting the slot value in transaction N, attacker makes transaction N+1's afterSwap compute a false price ratio that passes bounds check despite the actual swap price violating bounds
hypotheses.mechanism: AMMStandardHook.sol line 839: _setTstorish writes DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT. Lines 843-844: afterSwap reads it. No _clearTstorish is ever called on this slot. In tstore mode, the value auto-clears at tx end. In sstore fallback mode (Tstorish line 108: sstore(slot, value)), the value persists to block N+1.

Tstorish.sol: 106-109: sstore fallback — value persists across transactions
143-157: _clearTstorish exists but is NEVER called for DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT

attack_preconditions: Protocol deployed on chain without EIP-1153 support (sstore fallback mode active)
__activateTstore not called (or chain doesn't support it)
AMMStandardHook with price bounds configured on a token
Attacker can execute transaction N to set slot, then transaction N+1 to exploit stale value
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Protocol deployed on L2 without EIP-1153 (or before network upgrade). 2. Attacker executes swap with specific amount that sets slot to value V. 3. In next transaction, attacker executes swap with amount where actual price is out of bounds, but the stale slot value V causes computed ratio to appear in-bounds. 4. Bounds check passes despite price violation.
hypotheses.notes: Primary risk is on chains without EIP-1153. Cancun EVM (primary deployment target) has EIP-1153, so this is a secondary risk. However, the protocol's Tstorish pattern explicitly supports SSTORE fallback, suggesting cross-chain deployment is intended. The missing _clearTstorish call is a genuine oversight even if not immediately exploitable on Ethereum mainnet.

hypotheses.title: Output-based direct swap: afterSwap bounds check uses pre-fee amount, actual taker amount is post-fee (smaller)
hypotheses.summary: For output-based direct swaps, AMMModule._directSwap executes: (1) beforeSwap hook writes swapAmount (amountOut) to DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT, (2) _applySwapByOutputOutputFees reduces swapCache.amountOut by fees, (3) afterSwap hook reads slot (original amountOut) but params.amount also reflects the original value. The computed ratio uses the pre-fee amountOut. The taker actually receives post-fee (smaller) amountOut, so the actual execution price is worse than the ratio computed by the bounds check. Confirmed execution order at AMMModule.sol lines 1844-1846: beforeHooks → _applySwapByOutputOutputFees → afterHooks.
hypotheses.victim: Swap takers in output-based direct swaps — they receive a worse price than what the price bounds check validates
hypotheses.attacker_profit: For high-fee configurations, the attacker (as the taker) gets tokens at a validated 'good' price but the actual price received is worse due to fees applied after bounds check. Or a hook owner can set high fees to bypass price protections.
hypotheses.mechanism: AMMModule._directSwap: line 1844 _executeBeforeSwapHooks (writes pre-fee amountOut to slot), line 1845 _applySwapByOutputOutputFees (reduces amountOut), line 1846 _executeAfterSwapHooks (reads slot: pre-fee amountOut). Both params.amount in afterSwap AND the tstore slot reflect the pre-fee amounts. The bounds check verifies a price that doesn't reflect the actual execution price post-fees.
attack_preconditions: Output-based direct swap (inputSwap = false)
Token has both BEFORE_SWAP and AFTER_SWAP hooks enabled
Non-zero swap fees configured (protocol fee or hook fee)
Price bounds configured close to actual market price
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Token has price bounds configured as [P_low, P_high] where P_high = current market price + 0.1%. 2. Attacker executes output-based directSwap where pre-fee price is within bounds. 3. Protocol applies 5% fee, reducing actual amountOut. 4. Actual execution price = amountIn / (amountOut * 0.95) which exceeds P_high. 5. Bounds check passes because it used pre-fee amountOut. 6. Attacker receives tokens at price outside validated bounds.
hypotheses.notes: The magnitude of impact depends on the fee rate. At typical AMM fees (0.3%), the price deviation is small. At maximum allowed fees (up to 100% per Constants.sol), this could be significant. The execution order (beforeHooks → outputFees → afterHooks at lines 1844-1846) is confirmed; contrast with input swap order (beforeHooks → inputFees → afterHooks at lines 1836-1838) which is the same pattern.

hypotheses.title: _onTstoreSupportActivated copies stale SSTORE slot to TSTORE, poisoning bounds check on activation
hypotheses.summary: AMMStandardHook._onTstoreSupportActivated (lines 951-954) copies the SSTORE value at DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT to TSTORE. If __activateTstore is called when the SSTORE slot contains a non-zero value from a prior SSTORE-mode transaction, that stale value is now in TSTORE. The very first afterSwap call after activation will read the stale value instead of the current beforeSwap amount, producing an incorrect price ratio and potentially bypassing or incorrectly triggering bounds check.
hypotheses.victim: First swap after tstore activation on the affected token — could bypass price bounds or cause spurious revert
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Attacker can pre-stage a specific SSTORE slot value in one transaction, then call __activateTstore, then execute a directSwap where afterSwap reads the pre-staged value instead of the real amountIn.
hypotheses.mechanism: AMMStandardHook lines 951-954: assembly copies sload(DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT) to tstore. The Tstorish._onTstoreSupportActivated pattern was designed for reentrancy guards (copying NOT_ENTERED state), but for DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT it copies arbitrary operational state that should be zero at activation time.
attack_preconditions: Protocol deployed in SSTORE fallback mode (chain without EIP-1153)
EIP-1153 support later enabled (e.g., network upgrade)
Attacker can control the timing of __activateTstore call
DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT has a non-zero value from prior SSTORE-mode operations
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. AMMStandardHook deployed in SSTORE fallback mode. 2. Attacker executes directSwap, setting sstore slot to value V_attacker. afterSwap does NOT clear the SSTORE slot. 3. Attacker calls __activateTstore() in the SAME transaction as the next direct swap. _onTstoreSupportActivated copies V_attacker to TSTORE. 4. In that same transaction, afterSwap reads V_attacker from TSTORE instead of the actual beforeSwap amount — bounds check uses stale ratio.
hypotheses.notes: This requires __activateTstore to be called in the same transaction as a directSwap's afterSwap phase. Since __activateTstore requires tx.origin == msg.sender, a contract cannot call it atomically with a swap. The attack window is narrow: it requires either a direct EOA atomicity trick or a chain-upgrade race scenario.

hypotheses.title: afterSwapRefund unguarded: reentrancy into CLOBTransferHandler during WNATIVE withdrawal
hypotheses.summary: CLOBTransferHandler.afterSwapRefund() (line 315) has NO nonReentrant modifier, despite making an external call to IWrappedNativeExtended(WRAPPED_NATIVE).withdrawToAccount(executor, refundAmount) at line 322. If the WRAPPED_NATIVE implementation sends ETH to `executor` and `executor` is a contract, its receive() callback can reenter CLOBTransferHandler. Because afterSwapRefund did NOT acquire the reentrancy guard, all guarded functions (openOrder, depositToken, withdrawToken, closeOrder, ammHandleTransfer) see the guard as NOT_ENTERED and allow execution. An attacker can thus reenter openOrder() during a refund, potentially creating orders with double-counted token balances.
hypotheses.victim: CLOBTransferHandler accounting integrity — reentrant calls execute while refund is in-flight
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Reentrant openOrder() during afterSwapRefund: attacker creates an order using tokens that haven't yet been fully accounted for in the refund, potentially double-spending the refunded tokens or creating an order without corresponding collateral
hypotheses.mechanism: Execution path: AMM.swap() → CLOBTransferHandler.ammHandleTransfer() [nonReentrant: sets ENTERED on CLOBTransferHandler] → CLOBTransferHandler guard released by nonReentrantAfter → [later in same swap] AMM calls CLOBTransferHandler.afterSwapRefund() [NO guard acquisition] → WRAPPED_NATIVE.withdrawToAccount(executor) → executor.receive() → CLOBTransferHandler.openOrder() [nonReentrant: guard is NOT_ENTERED → PASSES]. The CLOBTransferHandler reentrancy guard is scoped to CLOBTransferHandler's tstore namespace, separate from the AMM's guard.

CLOBTransferHandler.sol: 315: function afterSwapRefund(address executor, address token, uint256 refundAmount) external {
316:     if (msg.sender != AMM) { revert ...; }  // ONLY check — no nonReentrant
323:             return;  // ETH sent to executor → executor.receive() called
490: function openOrder(...) external nonReentrant { ... }  // GUARDED but guard not set

attack_preconditions: Token involved in swap has WRAPPED_NATIVE as refund token
Executor is an attacker-controlled contract with a malicious receive() function
afterSwapRefund is called by AMM as part of swap execution (not within ammHandleTransfer's nonReentrant scope)
CLOBTransferHandler reentrancy guard is NOT_ENTERED when afterSwapRefund is called
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker deploys MaliciousExecutor contract that reenters CLOBTransferHandler.openOrder() in its receive(). 2. Attacker places a CLOB order with MaliciousExecutor as executor. 3. Swap executes; AMM triggers afterSwapRefund, sending WNATIVE refund to MaliciousExecutor. 4. WNATIVE calls MaliciousExecutor.receive(), which calls openOrder() with the refunded ETH as collateral. 5. The refund accounting hasn't completed yet; the openOrder call creates an order. 6. The outer afterSwapRefund continues; the ETH is now double-counted.
hypotheses.notes: Critical verification needed: (1) is afterSwapRefund called by AMM within or outside the ammHandleTransfer nonReentrant scope? If inside, the guard is still set and openOrder would revert. (2) Does WRAPPED_NATIVE.withdrawToAccount send ETH to executor directly (triggering receive()) or through some other mechanism? The WRAPPED_NATIVE address 0x6000030000842044000077551D00cfc6b4005900 suggests a custom deployment — need to verify its transfer semantics. Confidence depends heavily on (1).

hypotheses.title: _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) strips DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG mid-swap during queued fee execution
hypotheses.summary: _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers() at AMMModule.sol line 3190 calls _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS). This invokes TstorishReentrancyGuardWithFlags._setReentrancyFlags(0), which preserves only the ENTERED bit and zeroes all operation-specific flags (DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG=1<<6, SWAP_GUARD_FLAG=1<<2, POOL_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG, etc.). Any hook called via _transferHookFeesByHook during fee collection will see _isReentrancyFlagSet(DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG) == false, even though a direct swap is actively in progress. Hooks that use this flag to gate context-sensitive behavior (e.g., 'only perform X if not in a swap') can be triggered in the wrong execution context.
hypotheses.victim: Protocol correctness — hooks that guard behavior based on swap context flags execute with incorrect context signals during queued fee collection
hypotheses.attacker_profit: A malicious hook contract can be designed to perform expensive or state-mutating operations conditionally on the absence of DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG. When called during fee collection (where the flag is stripped), those operations execute during a direct swap they were designed to avoid.
hypotheses.mechanism: TstorishReentrancyGuardWithFlags._setReentrancyFlags (line 68-72): `flags = flags & ~(ENTERED | NOT_ENTERED)` → strips base bits. `currentGuard = _getTstorish(REENTRANCY_GUARD_STORAGE) & ENTERED` → preserves only ENTERED. `_setTstorish(REENTRANCY_GUARD_STORAGE, currentGuard | flags)` → writes ENTERED | 0 = ENTERED. Result: all operation flags stripped, only ENTERED bit survives. This happens at AMMModule line 3190 BEFORE iterating the fee queue. Any hook in the queue sees NO swap flags.

TstorishReentrancyGuardWithFlags.sol: 69:     flags = flags & ~(ENTERED | NOT_ENTERED);  // strips base bits from input

attack_preconditions: A token with hook that uses _isReentrancyFlagSet(DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG or SWAP_GUARD_FLAG) to gate behavior
That hook is also registered for fee collection (TOKEN_SETTINGS_HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG)
A direct swap triggers the hook, which queues fee collection
The queued fee execution calls back into the hook — now without DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG set
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker deploys a hook contract that behaves differently based on _isReentrancyFlagSet(DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG): when flag is false, it executes a privileged action (e.g., unlocks excess fees, modifies pool state, claims extra tokens). 2. Hook also implements fee collection. 3. Attacker triggers a direct swap to enqueue a fee collection. 4. _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers strips the swap flag (line 3190) then calls the hook's fee collection. 5. Hook detects 'no swap in progress' and executes the privileged action it was meant to gate.
hypotheses.notes: The severity depends entirely on whether any deployed hook actually uses _isReentrancyFlagSet(DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG) to gate behavior. The flag stripping is confirmed at line 3190. AMMStandardHook does NOT appear to check this flag internally — the risk is for custom hook implementations. The pattern is genuinely problematic for the stated hook API contract: if hooks can query operation context flags, those flags must be accurate during fee collection callbacks.

hypotheses.title: multiSwap cross-hop DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT stale read: hop N slot bleeds into hop N+1 afterSwap when N+1 lacks BEFORE_SWAP flag
hypotheses.summary: DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) in AMMStandardHook is written in beforeSwap and read in afterSwap but never cleared. In a multiSwap sequence, if hop N writes the slot in its beforeSwap and hop N+1 uses the SAME AMMStandardHook instance but has only TOKEN_SETTINGS_AFTER_SWAP_HOOK_FLAG (no BEFORE_SWAP flag), hop N+1's afterSwap reads the stale value from hop N. The computed sqrtPriceX96 = SqrtPriceCalculator.computeRatioX96(hopN.amount, hopN+1.amount) — mixing amounts from different hops — and is not the real price of hop N+1. This is DISTINCT from CP-001 (which concerns directSwap in sequential same-tx operations) and from H-transient-storage-01/02 (which concern a single direct swap with asymmetric flags on one token). This is a multiSwap multi-hop contamination where two different pools using the same hook instance interleave slot writes.
hypotheses.victim: Token owners/LPs whose pricing bounds in AMMStandardHook are expected to prevent sandwiching on hop N+1 of a multi-hop route
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Attacker crafts a multiSwap where hop 1 writes a favorable 'before' amount to the shared slot, and hop 2 (which lacks beforeSwap) reads that stale value in afterSwap. The computed price ratio reflects hop1.amount/hop2.amount rather than hop2.amount/hop2.amount, potentially passing bounds that the real hop 2 price violates.
hypotheses.mechanism: LimitBreakAMM.multiSwap iterates hops sequentially: for each hop, [beforeSwapHooks → poolSwap → afterSwapHooks] fully completes before the next. Within each hop, _executeBeforeSwapHooks writes DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT when the pool is a direct-swap pool (poolType==0) and the hook has BEFORE_SWAP. The slot is read (and computed into sqrtPriceX96) in _executeAfterSwapHooks when AFTER_SWAP flag is set and poolType==0. The slot is NEVER cleared. If hop N+1's pool has only AFTER_SWAP flag, it skips beforeSwap entirely — the slot still holds hop N's value when hop N+1's afterSwap runs.

AMMStandardHook.sol: 843-846: afterSwap reads slot, computes ratio — assumes slot was written THIS hop
LimitBreakAMM.sol: 266-320: multiSwap — sequential hop execution, no slot reset between hops

attack_preconditions: multiSwap with at least 2 hops
Hop N pool: direct-swap (poolType=0), token has both BEFORE_SWAP and AFTER_SWAP flags on AMMStandardHook A
Hop N+1 pool: direct-swap (poolType=0), token has ONLY AFTER_SWAP flag on the SAME AMMStandardHook A
Hop N+1 token has pricing bounds configured
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker identifies a multi-hop route: Pool A (A→B, hook=AMMStandardHook, both flags) → Pool B (B→C, same hook, AFTER_SWAP only). Token C has tight pricing bounds. 2. Attacker crafts hop1.amount = V such that V/hop2.actualOutput lies within token C's bounds. 3. Actual hop2 price = hop2.actualInput / hop2.actualOutput is outside bounds. 4. multiSwap executes: hop1 writes V to slot; hop2 afterSwap reads V, computes V/output (within bounds); check passes. 5. Attacker completes a large hop2 trade at a price that violates the token owner's stated bounds.
hypotheses.notes: Requires confirming that multiSwap hops execute in strict sequence (beforeSwap_N → poolSwap_N → afterSwap_N → beforeSwap_N+1 → ...) without any slot reset between hops. Also requires confirming that a single AMMStandardHook instance can be registered as hook for tokens in different pools. The key distinction from CP-001: this involves the multiSwap path, the slot is polluted within the same multi-hop call (not two separate txs), and the slot write source is a different pool's hook invocation — not a prior tx's directSwap.

hypotheses.title: collectHookFeesByHook routes to DIRECT (not queue) path mid-swap after SWAP_GUARD_FLAG erasure in executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers — enables out-of-order fee drain
hypotheses.summary: ModuleFeeCollection.collectHookFeesByHook() has NO nonReentrant modifier. It uses _isReentrancyFlagSet(SWAP_GUARD_FLAG) to decide between QUEUE and DIRECT transfer. Inside _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers(), _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) is called at AMMModule:3190 BEFORE the transfer loop, clearing SWAP_GUARD_FLAG. Any callback from a transfer inside the loop (ERC777, hook-as-recipient) that calls collectHookFeesByHook() sees SWAP_GUARD_FLAG=false and takes the DIRECT path — not the queue path. This is fundamentally different from H-transient-storage-07, which concerns custom hook contracts checking DIRECT_SWAP_GUARD_FLAG themselves. H-10 concerns the AMM's own collectHookFeesByHook routing logic and allows an attacker-controlled hook to drain additional fee buckets (different tokenFor/tokenFee pairs) via the direct path during the fee collection loop — outside the normal queue ordering, without those amounts ever being queued.
hypotheses.victim: Protocol fee accounting integrity — fee buckets not originally queued can be drained via direct path during swap execution
hypotheses.attacker_profit: Attacker-controlled hook drains accumulated fees from additional (tokenFor, tokenFee) pairs without queueing them during the original swap, bypassing the queue ordering mechanism. Also enables a DoS variant: if the callback requests amount > available for a second fee pair, the sub-call reverts, propagating back through the outer safeTransfer, reverting the swap.
hypotheses.mechanism: Call chain during fee collection: _executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers → _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) [AMMModule:3190] → REENTRANCY_GUARD_STORAGE = ENTERED|0 (SWAP_GUARD_FLAG=0) → _transferHookFeesByHook → SafeERC20.safeTransfer(tokenFee, recipient, ...) → callback in recipient/tokenFee contract → collectHookFeesByHook(tokenFor2, tokenFee2, recipient2, amount2) → check: _isReentrancyFlagSet(SWAP_GUARD_FLAG)=false, _isReentrancyFlagSet(LIQUIDITY_GUARD_FLAG)=false, _isReentrancyFlagSet(FLASHLOAN_GUARD_FLAG)=false → takes DIRECT path → _transferHookFeesByHook(msg.sender, tokenFor2, tokenFee2, ...) executes immediately. Note: nonReentrant guard (ENTERED bit) is still set, but collectHookFeesByHook does NOT check it — only custom flags are checked.

AMMModule.sol: 3190: _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS);  // ALL custom flags cleared — SWAP_GUARD_FLAG now 0
TstorishReentrancyGuardWithFlags.sol: 68-72: _setReentrancyFlags preserves ONLY ENTERED bit, zeroes all others
74-76: _isReentrancyFlagSet checks custom flags, NOT ENTERED bit

attack_preconditions: Hook contract is registered as fee manager (TOKEN_SETTINGS_HOOK_MANAGES_FEES_FLAG) for a token
Hook has accumulated fees in multiple (tokenFor, tokenFee) buckets
The hook or fee recipient is a contract that can receive callbacks (ERC777 tokensReceived, or hook IS recipient)
A swap triggers fee queuing for one bucket; executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers processes it
hypotheses.exploit_scenario: Drain scenario: 1. Attacker's hook accumulates fees in 3 buckets. 2. Swap queues bucket1. 3. executeQueuedHookFeesByHookTransfers: _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) clears SWAP_GUARD_FLAG. 4. Bucket1 transfer fires ERC777 callback in hook. 5. Hook calls collectHookFeesByHook for buckets 2 and 3 → DIRECT path → both drained. 6. Attacker extracts fees from 3 buckets in what should have been a 1-bucket queue flush. DoS scenario: If hook requests amount > bucket2 balance, revert propagates, bricking the swap and leaving all fees in an inconsistent state.
hypotheses.notes: High confidence because: (1) collectHookFeesByHook has NO nonReentrant modifier — confirmed at ModuleFeeCollection:72. (2) _setReentrancyFlags(NO_FLAGS) clears SWAP_GUARD_FLAG before the loop — confirmed at AMMModule:3190. (3) _isReentrancyFlagSet checks custom flags, not ENTERED — confirmed at TstorishReentrancyGuardWithFlags:74-76. (4) _transferHookFeesByHook calls safeTransfer which can trigger callbacks. CEI pattern in _transferHookFeesByHook prevents double-spend of the SAME bucket, but multiple DIFFERENT buckets can be drained. Exploitation requires callback-capable token or hook-as-recipient.

hypotheses.title: Dual-token AMMStandardHook: same slot written and read by both token hooks in one direct swap
hypotheses.summary: When BOTH tokenIn and tokenOut of a direct swap use the SAME AMMStandardHook contract address as their hook, all four hook calls (2x beforeSwap, 2x afterSwap) share a single DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT tstore slot (tstore is scoped per contract address). _executeBeforeSwapHooks at AMMModule lines 2370-2390 calls tokenIn's beforeSwap first, then tokenOut's beforeSwap — both writing the same swapAmount. However, _executeAfterSwapHooks calls tokenIn's afterSwap then tokenOut's afterSwap — each potentially passing a different params.amount. If the afterSwap for tokenIn and tokenOut receive different amounts (amountIn vs amountOut respectively), the second afterSwap call reads a slot value that was written by the first call's expected amount, not the second's, causing incorrect price ratio computation for one of the two tokens.
hypotheses.victim: Token owners who both configure the same AMMStandardHook — price bounds validation for one of the two tokens will use an incorrect amountIn/amountOut
hypotheses.attacker_profit: If the price bounds for tokenIn are validated using tokenOut's amount (or vice versa), the computed sqrtPriceX96 will be wrong — potentially allowing a swap that violates one token's bounds while satisfying the other's
hypotheses.mechanism: Both beforeSwap calls write the same swapAmount (AMMModule._executeBeforeSwapHooks line 2368: `swapAmount = inputSwap ? amountIn : amountOut`). The slot is overwritten twice with the same value, so no collision in beforeSwap. In afterSwap, both hook calls read from the same slot. The issue would manifest if afterSwap for tokenIn modifies the slot (it doesn't in the current implementation — there is no write in afterSwap path). Therefore the slot collision is BENIGN in the current implementation but creates a latent hazard for future changes.

AMMModule.sol: 2381-2390: tokenOut.beforeSwap called with same swapAmount — overwrites slot with same value

hypotheses.exploit_scenario: Currently benign: both tokenIn and tokenOut beforeSwap write the same swapAmount to the slot. However, if a future hook version writes different values per-token in beforeSwap, or if afterSwap receives different amounts per-token, the shared slot becomes a collision vector. This hypothesis documents the latent hazard rather than an immediately exploitable bug. The shared tstore namespace between two semantically-different hook invocations is an architectural smell.
hypotheses.notes: After confirming _executeBeforeSwapHooks at lines 2368-2390, the benign case is clear: both tokens receive identical swapAmount. The hypothesis should be downgraded from tracking to informational unless _executeAfterSwapHooks passes different amounts per token AND those amounts are used in slot writes. Recommend verifying _executeAfterSwapHooks implementation. LOW confidence for exploitability, but MEDIUM confidence for latent architectural risk.

summary.key_invariant_at_risk: AMMStandardHook price bounds enforcement for direct swaps depends on a two-phase tstore write (beforeSwap) + read (afterSwap) pattern, where each phase is independently gated by a separate token settings flag. This creates flag-asymmetry vulnerabilities (H-01: bypass, H-02: DoS) as the critical invariant. Secondary: the reentrancy guard tstore slot for the entire LimitBreakAMM proxy is manipulated (flag-stripped) during queued fee collection (H-07, H-10), creating context-signal integrity failures for hooks and the AMM's own routing logic.
summary.primary_attack_surface: DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT at 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF — written in beforeSwap, read in afterSwap, NEVER cleared. No enforcement that both hook flags must be set together (H-01, H-02). Also exploitable in multiSwap cross-hop scenarios (H-09). Secondary surface: REENTRANCY_GUARD_STORAGE operation flags stripped at AMMModule.sol:3190 during queued fee execution — affects both custom hook context checks (H-07) and the AMM's own collectHookFeesByHook routing (H-10).
known_bugs_excluded: CP-001 (HOOK-001): DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT stale read across same-tx operations — deliberately excluded per task constraints
summary.exploit_reference: SIR Trading transient storage exploit ($355K, Mar 2025): attacker exploited tstore slot persisting within same transaction. H-01/H-02 are simpler — they exploit the ABSENCE of writes/reads rather than stale intra-tx values. H-07/H-10 are closest to the SIR pattern: a flag slot is manipulated mid-transaction to produce incorrect control flow in downstream callers. H-09 is a multiSwap cross-hop variant of CP-001 operating on a different code path (multiSwap vs directSwap, same-tx within-call vs cross-operation).
